chapter_title: Annexes T to X (informative): laboratory testing of rock material and bibliography

sections.title: Preparation of specimen for testing on rock material
sections.summary: ISRM methods hold no general rock specimen preparation rule; X.4.8 gives common practice; weak or structured rock may miss ISRM criteria; samples 300 mm to 1000 mm long and over 50 mm diameter usually suffice; describe fissuring first; pack weak rock at once.
sections.body: (1) The ISRM Suggested Methods for Rock Characterisation, Testing and Monitoring contain no specific requirement for preparing rock specimens, though most test methods have a section on sample volume, quality, preparation method, dimensions and tolerance checks on dimensions and shape. (2) Examples of common practice for preparing rock core specimens and determining dimensional and shape tolerances are in the document listed in X.4.8; extracts and comments follow. (3) Specimens meeting the desirable ISRM criteria cannot always be obtained, e.g. in weaker, more porous and poorly cemented rock or rock with structural features. (4) Instruments for straightness, flatness and end perpendicularity should be controlled on a registered regular basis, with tolerances meeting at least the requirements of the specific rock tests. (5) Most unfractured cores from single, double or triple tube barrels by rotary drilling can be used, with or without re-coring after trimming the end bearing surfaces; blocks from the formation may also be used if their orientation is clearly marked for re-coring. (6) The sample volume depends on the test programme; for many purposes samples 300 mm to 1000 mm long with diameter greater than 50 mm suffice for a group of classification, strength and deformation tests. (7) The quantity of cores depends highly on natural and induced fissuring; the initial core description should evaluate fissuring and homogeneity and be used to select sections for testing. (8) Specimens from unfractured zones may not represent the formation; allow for this in reporting. (9) For weaker (sedimentary) rocks, sample treatment matters greatly for deformability, strength and swelling tests; pack samples in the field as soon as they leave the core barrel, since even short exposure may change water content and properties. (p. 170)
key_points: ISRM methods have no specific preparation requirement (p. 170).
Samples 300 mm to 1000 mm long, diameter > 50 mm usually suffice (p. 170).
Unfractured specimens may not represent the formation (p. 170).
Pack weak rock samples immediately in the field (p. 170).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Rock mass classification on cores needs the highest core recovery and least drilling disturbance, since most rock quality designations rest on core fractures; samples are at least 50 mm diameter, 50 mm to 200 mm of unfractured core suffices for element tests.
sections.body: (1) Classifying the rock mass on cores calls for the highest possible core recovery to identify discontinuities and possible cavities; minimise drilling disturbance since most rock quality designations relate to fractures in the cores. (2) Most classification systems relate to cores and rotary drilling samples of at least 50 mm diameter; for most tests 50 mm to 200 mm of non-fractured core suffices for element testing. NOTE 1: examples of tests are in the documents listed in X.4.9. NOTE 2: rock mass classification systems on semi-numerical methods exist for engineering, as summarised by Bieniawski (1989) Engineering Rock Mass Classification (see X.5). (p. 171)
key_points: Samples at least 50 mm diameter; 50 mm to 200 mm unfractured core (p. 171).

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Porosity (or void ratio) needs the density of solids, measured or estimated from local experience; closed pores need specialised analysis beyond powdered-sample solid density; avoid mercury displacement methods.
sections.body: (1) Porosity (or void ratio) calls for the density of solid particles, or an estimate from local experience with similar rock. (2) Closed pores may influence porosity; total pore volume may be based on the solid density of a powdered sample, but open and closed pore amounts call for specialised analysis. (3) Avoid methods using mercury displacement. NOTE: examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.9.3 (p. 172). (pp. 171 to 172)

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Test undisturbed rock for swelling where possible since fabric matters; weak or broken material such as joint fill may be remoulded and re-compacted, described in the report; Table V.1 sets at least three specimens per test type, doubled where swelling rock is likely.
sections.body: (1) Test undisturbed specimens where possible, since rock fabric strongly affects swelling; where the sample is too weak or broken to prepare, such as joint fill material, swelling index tests may use remoulded and re-compacted specimens, the procedures being described in the report. (2) Table V.1 guides the minimum number of swelling tests for different specimen dimensions, for sites with limited risk of swelling rock; where swelling is more likely increase the numbers to at least double those in the table; other advanced tests may better determine in-situ swelling. NOTE: examples of tests are in the documents listed in X.4.10. (p. 173)

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Follow ISRM or ASTM for uniaxial strength and deformability, Part 2 (adding Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio) preferred, with less strict amendments: platens D to (D + 10) mm, a spherical seat, H/D 2 to 3, diameter ≥ 50 mm, ends flat within 0,02 %, failure in 5 min to 15 min.
sections.body: (1) Follow the ISRM or ASTM methods as examples for uniaxial compressive strength and deformability testing, with the modifications of W.1. NOTE: see X.4.11.1. (2) The ISRM procedure has two levels: Part 1 for uniaxial compressive strength, Part 2 for deformability in compression. (3) The first gives the compressive strength, the second also the axial deformation modulus (Young's modulus) and Poisson's ratio, and is preferred. (4) The ISRM procedures are extremely difficult to meet, especially sample preparation and geometric tolerances; this annex's practice is less strict, setting minimum requirements, as more tests matter more than fewer tests on higher quality specimens. (5) Amendments to ISRM: platen diameter between D and (D + 10) mm, D the sample diameter, or greater if plate stiffness is sufficient, with special provisions to centre the specimen; at least one end platen with a spherical seat; right circular cylinders with height to diameter 2 to 3 and diameter not less than 50 mm, specimen diameter to largest grain as low as 6:1 in weak rock but 10:1 preferred; ends flat within 0,02 % of the diameter and perpendicular to the axis within 0,1°; no capping or end treatment other than machining except for soft rocks, where capping should be better than the rock (p. 175); diameter and height to the nearest 0,1 mm or 0,2 %, whichever is greatest; strain gauges at least ten times the grain size, on the middle third, or over the whole height if shown equivalent; constant stress or strain rate giving failure in 5 min to 15 min, excluding any load cycles; a machine of sufficient capacity loading at constant rate, with platen parallelism checked. (6) Initial deformations may include end bedding and closure of micro-cracks; total deformation from platen separation alone may give false deformation properties (p. 176). (pp. 175 to 176)
key_points: ISRM Part 2 (strength plus Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio) preferred (p. 175).
Platens D to (D + 10) mm; one spherical seat (p. 175).
H/D 2 to 3, diameter ≥ 50 mm, grain ratio 10:1 preferred (6:1 weak rock) (p. 175).
Gauges ≥ 10 grain sizes on the middle third (p. 176).

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Follow ISRM for rock direct shear with amendments: travel beyond expected dilatation, normal load held within 2 %, shear rate below 0,1 mm/min before readings, reconsolidation per normal stress; test plane preferably at least 2 500 mm2, grain ratio at least 10:1, joint to box size not below about 0,5.
sections.body: (1) Follow the ISRM method as an example. NOTE: see X.4.11.3. (2) Amendments: the machine travel should exceed the expected dilatation or consolidation and hold the normal load within 2 % of a selected value, with dilation measured as accurately as shear displacement; shear displacement rate below 0,1 mm/min in the 10 min before a set of readings, unless automatic logging makes this unnecessary; reconsolidate under each new normal stress and continue shearing to ISRM criteria, noting any cleaning or unloading before repositioning and describing removed material (p. 177). (3) Direct shear strength may also come from field tests, needing detailed assessment of the discontinuities. (4) Results serve, for example, equilibrium analysis of slopes and stability of dam foundations, tunnels and underground openings. (5) Cores or cut blocks may be used, with a test plane preferably at least 2 500 mm2; for unfilled joints the diameter or edge should preferably be at least 10:1 to the largest grain; joint length to shear box size not below about 0,5 to avoid instability of the apparatus. (6) Cut specimens with a large-diameter core drill or rock saw, avoiding percussive drills, hammers and chisels. (7) Orient the specimen so the shear plane is a plane of weakness (joint, bedding, schistosity or cleavage) or a soil-rock or concrete-rock interface (p. 178). (pp. 177 to 178)
key_points: Shear rate < 0,1 mm/min for 10 min before readings (p. 177).
Test plane preferably ≥ 2 500 mm2; joint/box size not below about 0,5 (p. 178).
No percussive drills, hammers or chisels (p. 178).

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Follow ISRM for the Brazil test: specimens of core size (D ≈ 54 mm) or more, thickness about the radius, irregularities within 0,025 mm, ends flat within 0,25 mm and parallel within 0,25°; anisotropic rock cut parallel and perpendicular to bedding.
sections.body: (1) Follow the ISRM method as an example. NOTE: see X.4.11.4. (2) Cut specimens with diameter D not less than the core size (D ≈ 54 mm) and thickness about equal to the radius; the cylindrical surface free from obvious tool marks; irregularities across the thickness not over 0,025 mm; end faces flat within 0,25 mm and parallel within 0,25°. (3) For shale and other anisotropic rock cut specimens parallel and perpendicular to the bedding, specifying the load direction for those cut parallel. (p. 178)
key_points: D not less than core size (D ≈ 54 mm), thickness about the radius (p. 178).
